title: HTML Text Formatting
summary: Inline elements that give words meaning: strong, em, mark, small, del and ins, sub and sup, code, abbr, time and more, and why meaning beats appearance.
introduction: HTML has a family of small inline elements for marking up words and phrases: importance, emphasis, highlighted text, deletions, abbreviations, code, dates. Most of them also change how the text looks, which tempts people to pick them for their appearance. The better habit is to pick the element for what the text *means* and let CSS handle the look. This lesson shows each element and the meaning behind it.
learningObjectives: Choose strong and em for meaning rather than b and i for looks
Mark up code, keyboard input, abbreviations, dates and edits correctly
Explain the difference between semantic and presentational formatting

blocks.text: Screen readers can convey `<strong>` and `<em>` with a change of tone; `<b>` and `<i>` carry no such meaning. When you want the reader to understand that something matters, use `<strong>`.

items: `<mark>` highlights text that is relevant in the current context, like a search match.
`<small>` is for side comments and fine print, not for making any text smaller.
`<del>` and `<ins>` show removed and inserted text, useful for change logs and corrections.

blocks.text: The `datetime` attribute on `<time>` gives machines a precise, language-independent value while people read the friendly text. Search engines use it for event and article dates.
`<span>` has no meaning at all; use it when you need to style or script a run of text and no semantic element fits, for example a coloured word in a logo.

Using `<strong>` to make a label bold or `<small>` to shrink a caption is a common mistake. If the only goal is appearance, use a `<span>` with a CSS class. The element should describe meaning, the stylesheet should describe looks.

questions.question: Which element should mark a keyboard shortcut such as Ctrl + C?
questions.explanation: `<kbd>` represents user keyboard input; `<code>` is for code, `<samp>` for program output.
